title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Problem Statement



RKR is moving from an instructional restaurant to a dual model that adds stand-alone service days (Kwok 2026).
Stand-alone days cannot rely on state funding, so they need steady reservations to stay viable (Kwok 2026).
The Collins Concierge already reaches faculty and staff, the segment that best fits RKR’s weekday lunch hours (The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch n.d.).



The gap
The RKR section is mostly text, and the “Reserve a Table” button sits at the bottom, below the hours.1 Readers who skim can scroll past it.



The business problem comes straight from Dr. Kwok’s proposal: the stand-alone service days need their own demand. The newsletter is the cheapest place to start because RKR already owns it and the audience is already on campus. The issue is the design: text heavy, button at the bottom.

Based on the team’s review of current Concierge issues, Fall 2026.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Analytics Objective

PO1: Strengthen the visual design of RKR’s section of The Collins Concierge to drive reservation growth.



AO1: Compare RKR click rates and attributed OpenTable reservations across RKR newsletter section designs, testing button placement in Fall 2026 and image versus video in Spring 2027.



Fall 2026 Move “Reserve a Table” to the upper left, compared with past issues
Spring 2027 A/B test image vs. video, with the button fixed in the upper left

One change at a time. Fall isolates placement. Spring isolates media. If both changed at once, there would be no way to tell which one moved clicks.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Importance



Reaches the primary segment
Faculty and staff rated highest in the team’s segment analysis, and the Concierge reaches them directly.


Low cost, already owned
No ad spend. The section runs every week, so each issue is a chance to test.


Measurable end to end
Canva tracks views and clicks; version-specific links can tie clicks to OpenTable bookings.



One change
at a time.




Clicks show interest, not bookings. Reservations remain the secondary, validating measure (Kumar 2021).

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Well-established Models








Framework
Key finding
What it means for AO1




Email response process
Newsletter response moves from seeing, to engaging, to acting; format tests against a control work well (Hartemo, Suomi, and Hakala 2016)
Use past issues as the control baseline


Relational vs. transactional metrics
Across 811 newsletters, clicks had the strongest link to eventual purchase (Kumar 2021)
Click-through rate is the primary metric


Visual heuristics
Readers scan newsletters in a U-shape; upper-left links earn higher CTR (Kumar and Salo 2018)
Fall moves the button to the upper left


Visual attention
Large images drew more attention than prices or codes, and attention mapped to purchase (Skourou and Spiliotopoulos 2024)
Spring tests image vs. video


Cognitive load
GIFs and emojis together raised unsubscribes, though neither hurt CTR alone (Bashirzadeh, Mai, and Faure 2022)
Add only one visual element at a time




Industry guides from Semrush and OpenTable point the same way: key information and a bold button near the top, strong food photos, and test one variable at a time over at least two weeks.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Challenges in the Literature



Inbox overload
University recipients reported about 30 bulk emails a week and trashed 22% of newsletters (Kong, Zhu, and Konstan 2021). Academics at one business school received 324 organizational bulk emails in a year (Bicudo De Castro 2025).



Email needs a clear role
Readers resisted email that did not fit their customer journey (Zunac, Miletic, and Kozina 2022).




Implication: A redesign may not move CTR if readers never reach the RKR section. AO1 tracks views alongside clicks to separate a design problem from a readership problem.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Adequacy of the Information


Strengths

Covers attention, button placement, media, and fatigue
Findings line up with industry guidance (Go 2024; Jones 2023)
Directly actionable for a newsletter section


Limitations

Industry guides come from companies selling services
The eye-tracking study had a small sample (Skourou and Spiliotopoulos 2024)
The email-role study was mostly female participants (Zunac, Miletic, and Kozina 2022)




The gap: No reviewed study looks at a restaurant section inside a university newsletter. Primary data from the Concierge fills it.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Need for Additional Analysis

Build a baseline of RKR click rates from past Concierge issues in Canva.
Fall 2026: measure the effect of moving the button to the upper left.
Spring 2027: alternate image and video issues weekly, button fixed.
Tag links by version so OpenTable bookings trace back to the design.
Flag unusual weeks such as holidays, finals, and campus events.


Clicks will not capture everyone. Walk-in guests and Bronco Bucks payers may never click, so a “How did you hear about us?” question at booking helps account for those visits.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Data and Sampling



Source: Canva website insights for The Collins Concierge, exported as one CSV per issue
Window: the last 12 weeks of issues
Sampling: all available issues in the window (non-probability, convenience)
Cleaning: 14 exports received; 1 byte-identical duplicate removed, leaving 13 issues




2,681


total page views across 13 issues





The “Reserve a Table” button links to the RKR website rather than straight to OpenTable, so clicks to cpp.edu/rkr pages are the measurable step before a booking.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Data Wrangling
Each export stacks four dimensions (country, device, source, link) in long format. The code below collapses them to one row per issue.

issue_summary <- issues |>
  group_by(issue) |>
  summarise(
    views       = sum(Count[Dimension == "country"]),
    mobile      = sum(Count[Dimension == "device" & Name == "Mobile"]),
    link_clicks = sum(Count[Dimension == "link"]),
    rkr_clicks  = sum(Count[Dimension == "link" &
                            str_detect(Name, "cpp\\.edu/rkr")]),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(ctr = rkr_clicks / views)


Lines 1 and 2: start from the stacked data and group by issue. Line 4: views come from the country rows, which sum to total page views. Lines 7 and 8: RKR clicks are any link to cpp.edu/rkr, which covers both the homepage and the menu page. Line 10: click rate is RKR clicks divided by views.

section: Baseline: RKR Click Rate by Issue

Baseline: RKR Click Rate by Issue


This is the pre-test baseline that Fall’s button move will be compared against. Clicks to RKR are low across the board, which is exactly the problem AO1 is designed to address.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Analytics Methods


A/B testing in two phases
Only one element changes per phase, so any difference in clicks can be traced to that change.
Two-proportion z-test
Compares click rates between conditions at α = 0.05:
\[z = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2}{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}}\]


Independent-samples t-test
Compares the average weekly OpenTable reservations attributed to each design.


Why these methods

The z-test is the standard way to compare two rates
The t-test fits weekly reservation counts across two groups
Together they follow the reader’s path from view → click → booking (Hartemo, Suomi, and Hakala 2016)

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
NoteAbout this report



This report reflects on Module 06. Section 1 covers my impressions of Reveal.js, Section 2 covers the presentation I built, and Section 3 walks through three data wrangling functions from the advanced wrangling lecture, using real data from my project.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
1.1 First Impression
My first impression was that Reveal.js turns a slide deck into a web page you can code, which I find both efficient and practical. Watching Dr. Lange build slides from a YAML header, and then Jarrod restyle an entire deck by changing one line in the theme, showed me that the design lives in settings and style files instead of in hundreds of manual clicks. That felt unfamiliar at first, since I usually design in Canva (I don’t particularly care for PPT – especially the online version – it’s very static and limited in its ability to manipulate), but it also felt more reliable. Once a style rule is written, every slide follows it.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
1.2 Capabilities
The workshop showed four groups of features. Each tab below summarizes one group.

StructureEngagementDesignCode and Data



YAML header: title, subtitle, author, theme, slide numbers, footer, and logo, all set in one place
Incremental lists: bullets appear one at a time, either globally or for one list
Manual pauses: three dots (. . .) reveal any content in steps, not just lists
Columns, asides, and footnotes: side-by-side layouts and small notes that stay out of the way
Scrollable and smaller slides: handle content that will not fit on one screen




Navigation menu and overview mode: jump to any section, and see sections stacked vertically under their headings
Speaker view: notes and a timer that only the presenter sees
Slide zoom and chalkboard: zoom into a detail or draw on the slide
Multiplex: the presenter controls what the audience sees on their own devices




Ready-made themes: a full restyle with one word, such as serif or moon
Sass variables and CSS: custom colors, fonts, and rules, so a deck can follow a brand guide
Transitions and fragments: zoom, fade, highlight, and dim effects for individual elements




Code chunks: R code runs when the slides render, so charts and numbers come straight from the data
Line highlighting: walk the audience through code one line at a time
Output location: show results on the next click or the next slide
Publishing: one command puts the slides on Quarto Pub or GitHub Pages

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
1.3 Compared With PowerPoint

Reveal.js versus PowerPoint







Area
Reveal.js
PowerPoint




Reproducibility
Charts and numbers update when the data changes
Charts are pasted in and go stale


Consistency
One style file controls every slide
Each slide can drift from the template


Sharing
A single link that opens in any browser
A file to email, often with version conflicts


Code
Runs and highlights live code
Code is pasted as text or images


Learning curve
Requires YAML, Markdown, and some CSS
Familiar point-and-click design


Fine visual control
Precise layouts take code and testing
Drag and drop anything anywhere


Collaboration
Works through Git and GitHub
Real-time co-editing in Microsoft 365



The biggest strength of Reveal.js is that it is reproducible. If The Collins Concierge sends a new export next week, my chart updates when I render. The main weakness is the learning curve. Small visual changes that take seconds in PowerPoint, such as nudging a logo, can take several renders to get right.

text:
2.2 Reproducible Chart
The presentation reads 14 Canva exports from The Collins Concierge, removes one duplicate file, and builds the chart below every time it renders. Figure 1 is the same chart rebuilt here from the same files.


Code
issue_summary <- concierge |>
  group_by(issue) |>
  summarise(
    views      = sum(Count[Dimension == "country"]),
    rkr_clicks = sum(Count[Dimension == "link" & str_detect(Name, "cpp\\.edu/rkr")]),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(ctr = rkr_clicks / views)

pooled <- sum(issue_summary$rkr_clicks) / sum(issue_summary$views)

ggplot(issue_summary, aes(factor(issue), ctr * 100)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#005030", width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = pooled * 100, colour = "#FFB81C",
             linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Concierge issue (oldest to newest)", y = "RKR clicks per 100 views") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 1: RKR click rate by Concierge issue, the baseline for the Fall 2026 test





Across 13 issues and 2,681 page views, readers clicked through to the RKR website 50 times, a pooled rate of 1.9%. These numbers are written with inline code, so they update with the data.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
2.3 What It Is About
The slides propose Analytics Objective 1 of my culminating experience project with The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch (RKR). RKR’s section of The Collins Concierge newsletter is mostly text, and its “Reserve a Table” button sits at the bottom. The proposal tests two design changes, one at a time:

Fall 2026: move the button to the upper left and compare click rates with past issues.
Spring 2027: alternate image and video versions of the section, with the button fixed.

The deck follows the full proposal storyline: problem statement, analytics objective, literature review, data and sampling, data wrangling, measures, the baseline chart, and analytics methods. It uses the serif theme, restyled with the Cal Poly Pomona brand colors from the CPP Design Toolkit.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
2.4 What I Learned

Real data surfaces real problems. The Canva exports had no issue dates and one duplicate file. Building the deck forced me to clean and document the data, which I would have skipped if I had pasted a chart into PowerPoint.
The measure has to match the button. The “Reserve a Table” button links to the RKR website, not straight to OpenTable. That changed my metric from reservation clicks to clicks to the RKR site, the step right before booking.
Styling is layered. A ready-made theme handles most of the design, a Sass file overrides colors and fonts, and a CSS file adds custom touches. Knowing which layer to edit saved a lot of time.
Publishing is part of the work. Setting the repo up as a Quarto website with GitHub Pages gave the whole module one clean link, and the same setup will work for the rest of the course.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
3.1 Mutating Join: left_join()
When to use it: when I have a main table and want to bring in extra information from a lookup table, without losing any rows from the main table. Rows with no match get NA, which makes gaps easy to spot.
Example: Canva only gives raw URLs. I wrote a small lookup table that labels each website by type, then joined it to the link data to see what Concierge readers click on most.


Code
site_types <- tribble(
  ~domain,                              ~link_type,
  "cpp.edu",                            "CPP website (incl. RKR)",
  "canvas.cpp.edu",                     "Canvas",
  "forms.cloud.microsoft",              "Forms and surveys",
  "forms.gle",                          "Forms and surveys",
  "docs.google.com",                    "Forms and surveys",
  "qualtricsxmnd4wcnjt2.qualtrics.com", "Forms and surveys",
  "eventbrite.com",                     "Events",
  "collinsgiving2026.eventbrite.com",   "Events",
  "secure6.saashr.com",                 "Jobs and careers",
  "careers.aramark.com",                "Jobs and careers",
  "cpp.joinhandshake.com",              "Jobs and careers"
)

links |>
  left_join(site_types, by = "domain") |>
  mutate(link_type = coalesce(link_type, "Other")) |>
  count(link_type, wt = clicks, name = "clicks", sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(share = scales::percent(clicks / sum(clicks), accuracy = 1)) |>
  kable()

Every link row survived the join. Links not in my lookup came back as NA, and coalesce() relabeled them as “Other.” The result shows that forms and surveys dominate reader clicks, which is useful context: the RKR section competes with a lot of calls to action in each issue.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
3.2 Filtering Join: anti_join()
When to use it: when I need to find what is missing. It returns rows from the first table that have no match in the second, without adding any columns. It is ideal for quality checks, such as finding records that were never matched.
Example: which Concierge issues produced zero clicks to the RKR website?


Code
all_issues <- concierge |> distinct(issue)

issues_with_rkr <- links |>
  filter(str_detect(url, "cpp\\.edu/rkr")) |>
  distinct(issue)

all_issues |>
  anti_join(issues_with_rkr, by = "issue") |>
  kable()





issue




1


2





Issues 1 and 2 had no RKR clicks at all. Rather than filtering on a count of zero, anti_join() answers the question directly: these issues exist in the full list but never appear in the list of issues with RKR clicks.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
3.3 Set Operation: intersect()
When to use it: when two tables have the same columns and I want only the rows they share. Unlike joins, set operations compare entire rows, so both inputs must have identical structures.
Example: which websites did readers click in both the first half of the window (issues 1 to 6) and the second half (issues 7 to 13)? These are the links that keep showing up, so they compete with RKR week after week.


Code
early <- links |> filter(issue <= 6, !is.na(domain)) |> distinct(domain)
late  <- links |> filter(issue >= 7, !is.na(domain)) |> distinct(domain)

intersect(early, late) |>
  arrange(domain) |>
  kable()
